sections.overview: Chondrocladia lyra is a deep-sea carnivorous sponge in the cladorhizid family. Its striking lyre-like form gave rise to the common names harp sponge and lyre sponge.
sections.identification: One or more upright, comb-like vanes rise from a central base, with evenly spaced branches bearing rows of tiny hooked filaments. The number and arrangement of vanes vary among observed individuals, so the tidy, symmetrical harp shape is not identical in every specimen.
sections.habitat: The species is known from the northeast Pacific, including Monterey Canyon and Escanaba Ridge off California. The specimens described in the original study came from about 3 316–3 399 m, on deep seafloor far below the sunlit zone.
sections.diet: Unlike most sponges that filter microscopic food, it snares small crustaceans with surface hooks and digests them externally.
sections.behavior: A stalk and root-like extensions anchor it to the deep seafloor.
sections.reproduction: Sponges generally reproduce sexually through gametes, with free-swimming larvae that settle; species-specific observations of this sponge’s reproductive cycle remain sparse. The general sponge pattern should not be mistaken for a detailed account of C. lyra.
sections.ecology: It is part of a broader cladorhizid lineage of carnivorous sponges, including other Chondrocladia that catch small animals with modified surface structures. Its unusual feeding mode shows that sponges can occupy predator roles in deep-sea food webs.
sections.conservation: There is not enough species-level population or trend information here to assign a conservation category. Deep-sea sampling has revealed only a limited number of specimens, which is a knowledge gap rather than proof that the species is rare or threatened.
